explain.say: Water flows fastest on the outside of each bend, wearing the bank away, and slowest on the inside, where sand and mud are dropped. So the loops grow bigger and loopier.

explain.say: Over time two outside bends eat towards each other until only a thin neck of land separates them. During a flood, the river bursts through the neck and takes the shorter, straighter path.

faq.q: How is an oxbow lake formed?
faq.a: A river meander grows until its neck becomes very narrow. In a flood, the river cuts straight through the neck, and deposits seal off the old loop, leaving a curved lake beside the river.

faq.q: Why does a river erode the outside of a bend?
faq.a: As water goes round a bend, the fastest, strongest flow swings to the outside, wearing away the bank. On the inside the water is slow and drops sand, building a beach called a point bar.

faq.q: Why is it called an oxbow lake?
faq.a: Its curved shape looks like the U-shaped wooden collar, called an oxbow, once put around the necks of oxen pulling ploughs.

faq.q: What happens to an oxbow lake over time?
faq.a: Without a river flowing through, it slowly fills with mud and plants. It becomes a marsh, then dry land, though you can still see its curved shape from the air.

faq.q: Where can you see oxbow lakes?
faq.a: Along slow, winding rivers on wide flat floodplains, like the Mississippi in the USA, the Amazon, and many rivers in Britain and India.

facts: Oxbow lakes are named after the U-shaped collar used on oxen.
The lower Mississippi River has many oxbow lakes along its floodplain.
